# ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents

Chenhao Zhang Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, The
Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen    Zhongan Wang
Affiliation: College of Artificial Intelligence, Zhejiang University   
Mingxuan Li Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, The Chinese
University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen    Hehe Fan Affiliation: College of
Artificial Intelligence, Zhejiang University    Zheng Zhu
Affiliation: GigaAI    Ming Li ^(†)^(†)thanks: Corresponding author:
Ming Li (ming.li@u.nus.edu). Affiliation: School of Artificial
Intelligence, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen

###### Abstract

On-policy self-distillation lets a language agent act as its own Teacher
by conditioning on privileged context such as skills written from its
own trajectories. Its guidance, however, is weighted by how much this
context shifts token likelihoods rather than by whether it improves
behavior, so errors in self-written skills return through later updates.
We propose environment-calibrated on-policy self-distillation, which
uses environmental outcomes to decide how much to trust the Teacher’s
current guidance and which self-written skills to reinforce.
Command-level advantages, estimated by comparing commands executed at
similar observations, scale each Teacher preference and reward
reflections and skills whose induced preferences favor higher-advantage
commands. Without skills at inference, 3B and 7B agents reach $`90.5\%`$
and $`93.3\%`$ macro success on seen ALFWorld tasks and $`75.5\%`$ and
$`80.5\%`$ success on WebShop. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, they outperform
GRPO under the same protocol by $`11.0`$ and $`7.6`$ points. Supervising
only executable commands rather than the Actor’s full response raises 3B
WebShop success from $`52.3\%`$ to $`75.0\%`$.

## 1 Introduction

Large language model agents solve multi-step tasks by issuing commands
and reading the resulting observations \[[1](#bib.bib1);
[2](#bib.bib2)\]. Reinforcement learning (RL) trains such agents from
environmental rewards, but sparse and delayed rewards say little about
which intermediate decisions produced an outcome \[[21](#bib.bib21);
[3](#bib.bib3)\]. On-policy distillation (OPD) adds token-level Teacher
preferences along trajectories generated by the policy
itself \[[5](#bib.bib5)\]. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) obtains
these preferences without a separate Teacher model: the policy acts as
its own Teacher when its context contains privileged information, such
as feedback or skills summarized from earlier attempts \[[7](#bib.bib7);
[8](#bib.bib8); [9](#bib.bib9)\]. When a model generates skills from its
own trajectories, every update supplies supervision for subsequent
learning. This creates an iterative learning loop. The performance of
this loop relies on whether the self-generated supervision is reliable.

In standard OPSD, however, nothing checks whether this supervision is
correct: each sampled token is weighted by how much the privileged
context changes its likelihood \[[7](#bib.bib7)\], whether or not the
change favors better behavior. This weighting can fail for agents in
three ways. The task may exceed what the Teacher knows, and an erroneous
Actor prefix may steer a capable Teacher toward the same
mistake \[[30](#bib.bib30); [31](#bib.bib31)\]. Teacher reasoning may
also rely on privileged information that the Actor never observes, so
imitating it can weaken reasoning grounded in the Actor’s own
observations \[[32](#bib.bib32)\]. When the policy writes its own
skills, a mistaken reflection can enter a skill and return through the
next policy update.

Calibration methods regulate the local signal, align decision contexts,
or tie Teacher weights to returns and policy
influence \[[18](#bib.bib18); [12](#bib.bib12); [6](#bib.bib6);
[13](#bib.bib13); [35](#bib.bib35)\]. Their assessment, however, does
not reach the process that generates the guidance. Methods that adapt
this process \[[14](#bib.bib14); [2](#bib.bib2); [10](#bib.bib10);
[11](#bib.bib11)\] do not train it on whether the resulting guidance
favors commands with better environmental outcomes. This raises a
question for skill-based self-distillation: can a single
environment-grounded criterion decide how much to trust the current
Teacher and also train the analysis that builds the next one?

![Refer to caption](2611.12232v1/figure1_environment_feedback.png)

Figure 1: Environmental outcomes help check an agent’s own advice. (a)
Self-generated advice can carry useful lessons and mistakes into later
training. (b) Our method uses observed outcomes to give useful advice
more influence and conflicting advice less influence. These outcomes
also train the generation of future advice. The comparison concerns how
advice is assessed during training.

Our method uses command-level environmental advantages both to weight
current Teacher guidance and to train the analysis that produces the
next Teacher.
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
illustrates the central contrast: using environmental outcomes to check
self-generated advice. After supervised initialization on externally
annotated reflections and skills, a single model acts in the environment
(Actor), writes reflections and a consolidated skill for each trajectory
group (Analyzer), and serves as the Teacher when conditioned on that
skill. The advantages compare commands executed at similar observations
and therefore do not depend on the Teacher. The Analyzer earns credit
when its skill induces preferences for higher-advantage commands, so the
Teacher’s task knowledge is learned rather than assumed.

In the Actor update, each Teacher preference is scaled by its agreement
with the advantage; guidance misled by an erroneous prefix loses weight
without being reversed. Direct Teacher supervision covers only
executable commands, so the Actor never imitates reasoning that depends
on the skill, and RL trains the full response.

We evaluate on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-3B and 7B backbones.
Across three evaluation seeds, the trained agents without skills or
online analysis at inference reach $`90.5\%`$ and $`93.3\%`$ macro
success on seen ALFWorld tasks and $`75.5\%`$ and $`80.5\%`$ success on
WebShop. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, they outperform GRPO under the same
protocol by $`11.0`$ and $`7.6`$ points. In 3B ablations, supervision
scope has the largest effect: extending Teacher supervision from
commands to the full response lowers WebShop success from $`75.0\%`$ to
$`52.3\%`$, and removing environmental feedback from both updates lowers
ALFWorld success by $`6.5`$ points. At the end of training, only
$`47`$–$`53\%`$ of the raw Teacher weight agrees with trajectory
outcomes, and modulation raises this share to $`57`$–$`74\%`$. Our
contributions are as follows:

1.  1.  We formulate skill-based self-distillation as a closed loop in which
        the policy writes the skills that condition its own Teacher, and
        argue that one environmental criterion should both weight current
        Teacher guidance and train the analysis that produces future
        guidance.
2.  2.  We instantiate this criterion with command-level advantages: they
        modulate Teacher preferences in the Actor update and reward
        reflections and skills in the Analyzer update, while Teacher
        supervision is restricted to executable commands.
3.  3.  Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop with 3B and 7B backbones show
        that the trained agents outperform GRPO on unseen tasks without
        using skills at inference, and ablations show that command-only
        supervision and environmental feedback each contribute.

## 2 Related Work

Environmental credit for agent learning. Outcome-based RL evaluates
complete trajectories, whereas credit assignment must distinguish the
decisions that produced their outcomes \[[16](#bib.bib16);
[22](#bib.bib22)\]. Return decomposition assigns delayed outcome credit
to earlier decisions \[[21](#bib.bib21)\]. For interactive agents,
grouping repeated or behaviorally similar visits makes local
alternatives comparable \[[3](#bib.bib3); [23](#bib.bib23)\];
propagating consequences through shared state potentials incorporates
their downstream effects \[[4](#bib.bib4)\]. These comparisons can
identify useful commands within failed trajectories. We use
environmental command credit to evaluate whether Teacher guidance favors
useful decisions.

On-policy distillation and experience-based self-improvement.
Experience-based self-improvement introduces a complementary problem:
how should previous interactions become reliable guidance for later
behavior? Reflection memories and reusable insights retain experience in
context \[[24](#bib.bib24); [26](#bib.bib26)\]; iterative revision and
trained self-correction modify subsequent responses or policy
behavior \[[25](#bib.bib25); [27](#bib.bib27)\]. OPD and
skill-conditioned OPSD transfer guidance along policy-generated
sequences \[[5](#bib.bib5); [7](#bib.bib7); [9](#bib.bib9)\]. Shared
Actor and Analyzer parameters let the policy and its analysis evolve
together, as in SEED \[[10](#bib.bib10)\]. Errors in that analysis can
nevertheless re-enter later updates, and models may struggle to
recognize errors in their own feedback without reliable external
evidence \[[19](#bib.bib19); [20](#bib.bib20)\]. We further optimize the
reflections and skills according to the environmental value of the
Teacher preferences they produce.

Calibration of self-generated supervision. Calibration concerns what
guidance is transferred and what evidence justifies its influence.
Decision-level semantic rewards can weight a full
response \[[34](#bib.bib34)\]; our direct Teacher loss instead covers
only executable command content. Local signal regulation, step-aware
supervision, and aligned decision contexts control where and how
strongly Teacher preferences enter learning \[[18](#bib.bib18);
[12](#bib.bib12); [17](#bib.bib17); [6](#bib.bib6)\]. Environmental
returns and objective influence provide criteria for judging their
usefulness \[[13](#bib.bib13); [35](#bib.bib35)\]. For training the
source of guidance, GRSD evaluates reflection quality through external
assessment \[[14](#bib.bib14)\]. Our R/S credit instead evaluates a
skill through agreement between its induced Teacher preferences and
environmental command advantages.

## 3 Method

Our method jointly trains an acting policy (Actor) and a
trajectory-analysis role (Analyzer). Direct Teacher supervision covers
executable commands, and environmental command advantages determine its
strength. Agreement between these advantages and skill-induced
preferences also provides training credit for reflection and skill
generation.

As shown in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Method ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents"),
offline supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initializes reflection and skill
generation in the model shared by the Actor and Analyzer. During online
training, the Actor collects trajectory groups, and the Analyzer
generates one reflection per trajectory and one consolidated skill per
group. The skill conditions the pre-update model to form the Teacher.
Joint Actor and Analyzer optimization updates the shared parameters for
the next iteration.

![Refer to caption](2611.12232v1/Figure2_Method_Aligned_20261103.png)

Figure 2: Environmental feedback connects acting with Teacher
construction. Offline annotations initialize reflection and skill
generation through SFT. Online, reflections $`u_{gj}`$ produce a skill
$`z_{g}`$, which conditions the pre-update policy to score Actor-sampled
tokens. Token gaps $`\delta`$ are summed into raw command gaps $`d`$;
the mean $`\bar{d}=d/L`$ determines a shared modulation multiplier,
which scales each command token’s own gap. Environmental advantages
calibrate this guidance and supply shared credit $`c_{g}`$ for
reflection and skill generation. Panel (a) omits group and trajectory
indices: $`o_{t+1}`$ is the observation returned after action $`a_{t}`$.

### 3.1 Preliminaries and shared-policy setup

Let $`x_{g}`$ denote task $`g`$ and $`\theta_{k}`$ the shared model
parameters at iteration $`k`$. Each update collects $`G`$ task groups,
with $`K=8`$ trajectories $`\{\tau_{gj}\}_{j=1}^{K}`$ sampled from the
Actor $`\pi_{\theta_{k}}`$. At interaction step $`t`$, the Actor
generates response $`y_{gjt}`$ from history $`h_{gjt}`$. Its executable
command specifies action $`a_{gjt}`$, after which the environment
returns observation $`o_{gj,t+1}`$. We use $`\ell`$ for a response-token
index.

GRPO derives group-relative advantages
$`\widehat{A}^{\mathrm{RL}}_{gj}`$ from recorded episode
rewards \[[22](#bib.bib22)\]. Let $`\mathcal{B}_{A}`$ contain the valid
generated Actor-token indices $`(g,j,t,\ell)`$. The likelihood ratio is

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\rho_{gjt\ell}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{gjt\ell}\mid h_{gjt},y_{gjt,<\ell})}{\pi_{\theta_{k}}(y_{gjt\ell}\mid h_{gjt},y_{gjt,<\ell})}.
``` |  | (1) |

The clipped policy component of the GRPO objective is

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}^{\mathrm{policy}}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_{A}|}\sum_{(g,j,t,\ell)\in\mathcal{B}_{A}}`$ |  | (2) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\min\!\left\{\begin{aligned} &\rho_{gjt\ell}(\theta)\operatorname{sg}(\widehat{A}^{\mathrm{RL}}_{gj}),\\
&\operatorname{clip}\bigl(\rho_{gjt\ell}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\bigr)\operatorname{sg}(\widehat{A}^{\mathrm{RL}}_{gj})\end{aligned}\right\},`$ |  |  |

where $`\epsilon=0.2`$ and $`\operatorname{sg}`$ denotes
stop-gradient \[[16](#bib.bib16)\]. This token-mean objective trains the
complete generated response, including reasoning. We use
$`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}`$ for this policy loss plus a
frozen-reference KL penalty with coefficient $`0.01`$ and minus an
entropy bonus with coefficient $`0.001`$.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Implementation and training ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
gives the optimization settings.

The Analyzer uses the same parameter snapshot under reflection and
skill-generation prompts, denoted by $`R_{\theta_{k}}`$ and
$`S_{\theta_{k}}`$. Reflection generation produces one text $`u_{gj}`$
from each trajectory and its recorded outcome $`r_{gj}`$. Skill
generation consolidates these reflections into one text $`z_{g}`$:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle u_{gj}`$ | $`\displaystyle\sim R_{\theta_{k}}(\cdot\mid x_{g},\tau_{gj},r_{gj}),`$ |  | (3) |
|  | $`\displaystyle z_{g}`$ | $`\displaystyle\sim S_{\theta_{k}}\bigl(\cdot\mid x_{g},\{u_{gj},r_{gj}\}_{j=1}^{K}\bigr).`$ |  | (4) |

For task group $`g`$, the skill-conditioned Teacher is the pre-update
policy evaluated with $`z_{g}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi_{T,k}(\cdot\mid h_{gjt},y_{gjt,<\ell})\equiv\pi_{\theta_{k}}(\cdot\mid h_{gjt},z_{g},y_{gjt,<\ell}).
``` |  | (5) |

Both branches score the same Actor-sampled token under the same
reasoning prefix. Their token-level log-probability gap is

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\delta_{gjt\ell}={}`$ | $`\displaystyle\log\pi_{T,k}(y_{gjt\ell}\mid h_{gjt},y_{gjt,<\ell})`$ |  | (6) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle-\log\pi_{\theta_{k}}(y_{gjt\ell}\mid h_{gjt},y_{gjt,<\ell}).`$ |  |  |

In the sampled-token policy-gradient formulation of OPSD, the
uncalibrated coefficient is the likelihood gap itself \[[5](#bib.bib5);
[7](#bib.bib7)\]:

|     |                                               |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       w^{\mathrm{base}}_{gjt\ell}=\delta_{gjt\ell}.
       ```                                            |     | (7) |

This coefficient measures how privileged context changes token support.
It does not explicitly calibrate that support using the environmental
value of the corresponding command.

### 3.2 Environmental command credit

GRPO assigns the same trajectory-level advantage to every command in an
episode, so it cannot distinguish useful decisions within a failed
trajectory. We estimate a separate command-level advantage by comparing
commands executed at similar observations.

Commands are compared within states formed by representation-based
observation grouping \[[23](#bib.bib23)\]. Within each task group, we
use frozen-reference embeddings and require identical admissible-action
sets. A visit joins the nearest normalized-centroid cluster within
cosine distance $`0.1`$, or creates a new cluster. Recorded commands
connect these clusters through their observed successor states and
rewards.

![Refer to caption](2611.12232v1/environmental_credit_polished_v57.png)

Figure 3: An empirical transition graph provides environmental command
credit. Recorded observations are grouped into comparable state
clusters, and executed commands connect them through observed
transitions. Bellman evaluation estimates state values;
temporal-difference residuals then enter GAE and group standardization
to obtain command advantages. Colors identify observation clusters.

For transition $`i`$, let $`s_{i}`$ and $`s_{i}^{+}`$ denote its current
and successor clusters, with transition reward $`r_{i}`$. We initialize
$`V^{(0)}(s)`$ from the mean observed return-to-go and apply empirical
Bellman backups \[[33](#bib.bib33)\]:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
V^{(n+1)}(s)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}_{s}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{V}_{s}}\bigl[r_{i}+\gamma V^{(n)}(s_{i}^{+})\bigr],
``` |  | (8) |

where $`\mathcal{V}_{s}`$ contains the recorded visits to $`s`$ and
$`\gamma=0.95`$. Terminal and horizon successors have value zero. The
backups propagate observed downstream consequences into the values used
for local comparisons.

The temporal-difference residual is

|     |                                           |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       b_{i}=r_{i}+\gamma V(s_{i}^{+})-V(s_{i}).
       ```                                        |     | (9) |

Along each recorded trajectory, generalized advantage
estimation \[[15](#bib.bib15)\] propagates these residuals:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
B_{gjt}=b_{gjt}+\gamma\lambda_{\mathrm{GAE}}B_{gj,t+1},\qquad\lambda_{\mathrm{GAE}}=0.8,
``` |  | (10) |

with a zero tail value. Group standardization yields the auxiliary
command advantage $`\widehat{A}_{gjt}`$. It supplies Teacher modulation
and Analyzer credit, whereas $`\widehat{A}^{\mathrm{RL}}_{gj}`$ supplies
the primary GRPO update.
Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Environmental advantage estimation ‣ Appendix A Supplementary method details ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
gives the solver and normalization details.

### 3.3 Environment-calibrated self-distillation

Privileged skills can support executable decisions even when their
associated reasoning targets are unavailable to the Actor. We therefore
restrict direct Teacher supervision to command content. Let
$`\mathcal{C}_{gjt}`$ contain the positions in $`y_{gjt}`$ that encode
the executable command for action $`a_{gjt}`$, excluding delimiter tags,
and let $`L_{gjt}=|\mathcal{C}_{gjt}|`$. We retain the raw summed gap
for R/S credit:

|     |                                                          |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       d_{gjt}=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{C}_{gjt}}\delta_{gjt\ell}.
       ```                                                       |     | (11) |

The mean command gap used to compute the modulation multiplier is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{d}_{gjt}=\frac{1}{L_{gjt}}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{C}_{gjt}}\delta_{gjt\ell}=\frac{d_{gjt}}{L_{gjt}},
``` |  | (12) |

with $`\bar{d}_{gjt}=0`$ for empty command spans.

Environmental credit and the mean command gap determine a shared
modulation multiplier:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle m_{gjt}`$ | $`\displaystyle=1+\alpha_{m}\operatorname{sign}(\bar{d}_{gjt})\tanh\!\left(\frac{\widehat{A}_{gjt}}{\kappa_{m}}\right),`$ |  | (13) |
|  | $`\displaystyle w_{gjt\ell}`$ | $`\displaystyle=q_{g}\,\mathbb{1}[\ell\in\mathcal{C}_{gjt}]\,m_{gjt}\delta_{gjt\ell},`$ |  |  |

with $`\alpha_{m}=1`$ and $`\kappa_{m}=0.5`$. The multiplier lies in
$`[0,2]`$. Matching signs of $`\bar{d}_{gjt}`$ and $`\widehat{A}_{gjt}`$
strengthen the guidance, and conflicting signs attenuate it without
reversing individual token-gap directions. When $`\widehat{A}_{gjt}=0`$,
$`m_{gjt}=1`$ recovers the unmodulated token gaps. Each command shares
this multiplier across its content tokens, while each token retains its
own gap.

The group mask $`q_{g}`$ is one in ALFWorld. In WebShop, it is zero when
all eight trajectories succeed and one otherwise. The resulting weights
combine command-only supervision, a shared command-level multiplier, and
token-specific gaps.

For likelihood ratio $`\rho`$ and signed weight $`w`$, define the
clipped token loss

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{clip}}(\rho;w)=`$ |  | (14) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle-\min\!\left\{\begin{aligned} &\rho\,\operatorname{sg}(w),\\
&\operatorname{clip}(\rho,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\operatorname{sg}(w)\end{aligned}\right\}.`$ |  |  |

Using the Actor token-mean reduction, the calibrated OPSD objective is

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPSD}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_{A}|}\sum_{(g,j,t,\ell)\in\mathcal{B}_{A}}`$ |  | (15) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{clip}}\bigl(\rho_{gjt\ell}(\theta);w_{gjt\ell}\bigr).`$ |  |  |

The weights select command content, while the primary GRPO objective
continues to train the complete response.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Supplementary method details ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
derives the modulation properties.

### 3.4 Credit for reflection and skill generation

Command calibration evaluates a given Teacher signal. Training the
Analyzer additionally requires evaluating the reflections and skill that
produced it. We assign credit according to whether the skill shifts
support toward higher-advantage commands at comparable observations. The
reflection and skill prompts are provided in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Implementation and training ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents").

Within task group $`g`$, let $`\mathcal{I}_{g}`$ contain the
deduplicated transitions with valid command spans, and write
$`i=(j,t)`$. Let $`N_{g}`$ be the number of represented trajectories and
$`L_{gj}`$ the number of eligible transitions in trajectory $`j`$. We
use

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\omega_{i}=\frac{1}{N_{g}L_{gj}},\qquad\overline{A}_{g}(s)=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{g}:s_{i}=s}\omega_{i}\widehat{A}_{i}}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{g}:s_{i}=s}\omega_{i}}.
``` |  | (16) |

Each trajectory receives equal total weight, divided among its eligible
transitions. State centering gives
$`\Delta\widehat{A}_{i}=\widehat{A}_{i}-\overline{A}_{g}(s_{i})`$. This
comparison measures relative command value within a cluster rather than
differences in the average advantage of visited states.

The raw and bounded group credits are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
C_{g}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{g}}\omega_{i}\,\Delta\widehat{A}_{i}\,d_{i},\qquad c_{g}=\operatorname{clip}(C_{g},-3,3).
``` |  | (17) |

Here $`C_{g}`$ is a weighted within-state covariance between
environmental advantage and the raw summed Teacher preference $`d_{i}`$.
Positive credit reinforces analysis whose Teacher relatively supports
higher-advantage commands; negative credit discourages the reverse
association.

Because the skill consolidates the full reflection group, all $`K`$
reflections and the skill receive the same reward $`c_{g}`$. For an
analysis response $`v`$ generated under prompt $`p_{v}`$, define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho^{v}_{\ell}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(v_{\ell}\mid p_{v},v_{<\ell})}{\pi_{\theta_{k}}(v_{\ell}\mid p_{v},v_{<\ell})}.
``` |  | (18) |

Let $`\mathcal{M}_{v}`$ contain its valid generated-token positions. The
response-sequence mean loss uses the same clipped form:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{P}(v;c_{g})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}_{v}|}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{M}_{v}}\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{clip}}\bigl(\rho^{v}_{\ell}(\theta);c_{g}\bigr).
``` |  | (19) |

The Analyzer objective is

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{RS}(\theta)={}`$ | $`\displaystyle\frac{1}{2GK}\sum_{g=1}^{G}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\mathcal{P}(u_{gj};c_{g})`$ |  | (20) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2G}\sum_{g=1}^{G}\mathcal{P}(z_{g};c_{g}).`$ |  |  |

Reflection and skill generation each receive half of the total Analyzer
weight.

### 3.5 Joint optimization and iterative updates

The shared model is optimized with

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)+\beta_{T}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPSD}}(\theta)+\beta_{RS}\mathcal{L}_{RS}(\theta).
``` |  | (21) |

The GRPO term trains task behavior from environmental outcomes, the OPSD
term transfers calibrated command preferences, and the R/S term trains
the analysis producing those preferences. Actor and Analyzer gradients
accumulate at shared optimizer steps. Teacher gaps, advantages,
modulation weights, and group credits remain fixed during optimization.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Implementation and training ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
gives the coefficients and optimizer settings.

The updated parameters generate the next trajectories, reflections, and
skills:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\theta_{k}\longrightarrow\{\tau_{gj},u_{gj},z_{g}\}_{g,j}`$ |  | (22) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\longrightarrow\{w_{gjt\ell},c_{g}\}\longrightarrow\theta_{k+1}.`$ |  |  |

Each iteration therefore updates both the acting policy and the analysis
used to construct its subsequent Teacher.
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ A.1 Training algorithm ‣ Appendix A Supplementary method details ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
in
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Training algorithm ‣ Appendix A Supplementary method details ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
summarizes the update. At inference time, the Actor uses only the
ordinary interaction history.

## 4 Experiments

We evaluate agent performance across two environments and model sizes,
followed by generalization to unseen tasks. We then examine how
environmental feedback calibrates Teacher supervision and evaluates the
reflections and skills that construct it. The ablation study considers
initialization, supervision scope, and the two feedback paths with the
3B backbone.

### 4.1 Experimental setup

#### Benchmarks and metrics.

We evaluate on ALFWorld \[[28](#bib.bib28)\] and
WebShop \[[29](#bib.bib29)\], which test sequential interaction in
household and shopping environments. ALFWorld contains six task
categories: object placement, inspection, cleaning, heating, cooling,
and two-object placement. We use all 140 seen and 134 unseen evaluation
tasks and report category success and its unweighted macro average. Each
WebShop evaluation uses 128 tasks sampled without replacement from the
500-task held-out test set. We report exact task Success and mean
normalized environment Score on a 0–100 scale.

#### Models and training.

We use Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as our backbones. For
SFT, we collect eight trajectories for each of 200 training tasks.
WebShop collection uses a policy trained for 40 GRPO updates to obtain
sufficient successful and failed trajectories. GPT-6.1 sol annotates
each task group with eight reflections and one consolidated skill. We
fine-tune reflection and skill generation for three epochs, then train
the shared Actor and Analyzer for 150 online updates. In matched-batch
profiling with the 3B model, our method took approximately $`30\%`$
longer than GRPO.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Implementation and training ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
gives the initialization details and training hyperparameters.

#### Baselines.

We compare training-free prompting (Vanilla and Skill-Prompt\*),
reward-based learning (GRPO and Skill-GRPO), and distillation-based
learning (OPSD, GRPO+OPSD, Skill-SD, RLSD, SDAR, and AlignOPSD). An
asterisk denotes skill-conditioned inference. Published results come
from AlignOPSD Table 1 \[[6](#bib.bib6)\]; local measurements are
identified separately. Published ALFWorld averages retain their source
reporting conventions.
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Baseline details ‣ Appendix C Baselines, benchmarks, and evaluation setting ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
describes each method.

#### Evaluation protocol.

We evaluate our models and ablation variants at the final checkpoint
after 150 online updates. The Actor receives the ordinary interaction
history, without skill retrieval or online reflection and skill
generation. Training uses a fixed random seed throughout. For the main
and unseen-task comparisons, we evaluate each trained checkpoint under
three evaluation seeds and report means and sample standard deviations.
Each seed uses temperature 0.4 and one trajectory per task. ALFWorld
permits at most 30 actions with history length five; WebShop permits at
most 15 actions with history length two.
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Baselines, benchmarks, and evaluation setting ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
specifies the task panels, inference settings, and reporting
conventions.

Table 1: Comparison with published methods. ALFWorld reports category

model size, including ties.

#### The full method improves performance over GRPO.

Our full training scheme combines R/S SFT initialization with online
Actor and Analyzer optimization. Relative to the published GRPO
baseline, this scheme improved performance at both scales and in both
environments. WebShop Success increased by $`12.2`$ and $`7.9`$
percentage points for 3B and 7B, respectively. On ALFWorld, the
improvements covered five categories at 3B and all six at 7B.

#### Training-time skill guidance supports deployment with ordinary histories.

Skill-Prompt\* supplies strategies as inference context; our Actor
instead learns from skill-conditioned Teacher preferences during
training. The Actor exceeded Skill-Prompt\* on all six aggregate
comparisons and Skill-GRPO\* on five. These comparisons support
transferring useful guidance into a policy evaluated with ordinary
interaction histories, without skill retrieval or online analysis. The
exception was 7B WebShop Success, where skill-conditioned Skill-GRPO\*
remained stronger.

The unseen split tests transfer to new task instances within the same
six ALFWorld categories. We retain the original interaction protocol and
compare with the GRPO baseline in

The 3B and 7B Actors improved unseen macro success over their respective
GRPO baselines by $`11.03`$ and $`7.62`$ percentage points. The 3B model
remained below GRPO on Pick and Cool and matched it on Clean. The 7B
model remained below GRPO on Pick and Clean. These results suggest that
training supports reusable behavioral strategies that transfer to unseen
tasks. The 7B macro average was $`0.74`$ percentage points above 3B.

### 4.3 Mechanistic analysis

We examine how environmental feedback shapes Actor supervision and the
analysis used to construct its Teacher.
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Mechanistic analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
shows how modulation redistributes Teacher weight and how R/S credit
relates to the usefulness of skill-induced preferences.

Figure 4: Environmental feedback calibrates Actor supervision and
evaluates Teacher construction. (a,b) Reward alignment of Teacher
supervision before and after modulation. (c,d) Return concordance of
skills grouped by each task’s median R/S credit.

#### Modulation shifts Teacher weight toward reward-supported directions.

Reward alignment is
$`100\frac{\sum_{i}|w_{i}|\mathbf{1}[w_{i}\widehat{A}_{i}^{\mathrm{RL}}>0]}{\sum_{i}|w_{i}|}`$,
where $`w_{i}`$ is the raw or modulated Teacher weight and
$`\widehat{A}_{i}^{\mathrm{RL}}`$ is the trajectory-level GRPO advantage
associated with command $`i`$. We count each command once. The two
conditions use the same pre-update commands with
$`|\widehat{A}_{i}^{\mathrm{RL}}|>10^{-8}`$. The stored GRPO advantages
are obtained by standardizing episode outcomes, including the $`0.1`$
invalid-command penalty, within each task group.

We recorded nine snapshots per environment. Raw alignment on ALFWorld
declined over training, but modulation maintained higher alignment at
every recorded snapshot in both environments
(Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Mechanistic analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")(a,b)).
At update 150, modulation raised alignment from $`47.34\%`$ to
$`57.16\%`$ on ALFWorld and from $`53.46\%`$ to $`73.52\%`$ on WebShop,
gains of $`9.82`$ and $`20.06`$ percentage points. The multiplier
preserved preference signs and placed greater relative weight on
guidance consistent with observed rewards.

#### R/S credit favors skills with return-consistent Teacher preferences.

Return concordance compares raw Teacher–Actor command gaps with observed
returns-to-go. We paired distinct commands across trajectories with
identical Actor prompts and admissible-action sets. Teacher scoring
retains the reasoning prefix sampled in each response. Concordant and
discordant orderings score one and zero; preference ties score one-half,
and return ties are excluded. The metric averages pairs within each
skill and weights skills equally. Pooling saved snapshots after update 1
yielded 135 eligible ALFWorld skills and 88 WebShop skills. We split
each task at its median R/S credit and assigned median ties to the
lower-credit group.
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Mechanistic analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")(c,d)
shows individual skills, group means, and interquartile ranges.

Higher-credit skills achieved $`65.41\%`$ concordance versus $`57.83\%`$
on ALFWorld, and $`55.54\%`$ versus $`37.13\%`$ on WebShop. Higher R/S
credit was associated with skills whose Teacher preferences better
distinguished commands by their returns. Across training, success
increased and interactions shortened at both model scales.
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Training dynamics ‣ Appendix D Mechanistic analysis and training dynamics ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
presents the separate 3B and 7B curves together with modulation coverage
and positive-credit skill fractions.

Table 3: Ablation study on ALFWorld and WebShop with the 3B backbone.
Our ALFWorld branches report six-category macro success (140 tasks);
GRPO retains the published Avg. from
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Overall agent performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents").

#### SFT provides a useful starting point for online analysis.

Variant (a) tests whether the online loop can learn effectively without
initial trajectory-analysis SFT. The no-SFT variant still exceeded GRPO
on WebShop by $`6.23`$ percentage points in Success. SFT provided
further gains: the full method exceeded this variant by $`9.40`$
percentage points on ALFWorld and $`5.47`$ on WebShop Success. The
residual gain without SFT and the further gain with SFT suggest that
initialization and online guidance contribute at different stages.

#### Command-only supervision outperforms full-response matching.

Variant (b) tests whether matching Teacher reasoning adds value beyond
supervising executable commands. Extending the loss to the full response
reduced ALFWorld macro success by $`1.66`$ percentage points and WebShop
Success by $`22.66`$ percentage points. The Teacher’s reasoning uses
privileged skills unavailable to the Actor, so these additional targets
can impose context-specific preferences. The comparison favors
transferring executable decisions through the Teacher objective and
retaining environmental RL for the Actor’s complete response.

#### Environmental feedback improves skill-guided learning.

Variant (c) retains command-only Teacher supervision and online
reflection and skill generation in both environments. It removes only
environmental modulation and the direct R/S objective. It reached
$`85.00\%`$ ALFWorld macro success and $`72.65\%`$ WebShop Success, with
a WebShop Score of $`82.10`$. The full method improved macro success and
WebShop Success by $`6.54`$ and $`2.35`$ percentage points,
respectively. This joint ablation supports the combined value of
environmental modulation and R/S learning.

## 5 Discussion

The skill diagnostics provide a second view of improvement beyond final
task success. Higher-credit skills induced preferences that better
distinguished commands by their returns in both environments. This
association supports evaluating a generated lesson through the decisions
it favors. It also motivates tracking the usefulness of self-generated
advice as the policy and its experience change over training.

Evaluation without skills and the supervision-scope ablation show that
useful behavior can transfer from privileged experience to an Actor
operating with ordinary observations. The gap between command-only and
full-response supervision was larger on WebShop than on ALFWorld. This
difference suggests that the choice of supervision targets matters
across environments. The results favor transferring decisions that
remain executable with the information available to the Actor at
deployment.

## 6 Conclusion

We introduced ECOS to connect agent learning with the supervision
generated from its own interaction experience. The approach transfers
skill-conditioned guidance through executable commands and retains
reinforcement learning over the complete response. Environmental
feedback links the weighting of Teacher preferences to the optimization
of reflection and skill generation. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop
show improvements over reward-based baselines at both model scales,
together with transfer to unseen ALFWorld tasks. The evaluated Actor
requires no privileged skills or online analysis at deployment.
Mechanistic diagnostics show improved reward alignment of supervision
and more return-consistent guidance among higher-credit skills. Within
the tested settings, environmental outcomes provide a shared criterion
for policy improvement and the generation of future supervision.

## Limitations

Our environmental credit depends on estimated command values and
comparisons between observations. Sparse rewards or imperfect state
matching can bias both Actor and Analyzer updates. The current
diagnostics characterize agreement on recorded experience and do not
independently establish improvements in Teacher capability or reasoning
quality. SFT initialization relies on annotations from an external
model. Evaluation covers two text-based environments and Qwen2.5
backbones at 3B and 7B. Transfer to substantially longer
self-improvement runs remains untested. Reflection and skill generation,
together with Teacher rescoring, also introduce training overhead.
Independent skill evaluations and longer controlled runs would clarify
whether improved task performance accompanies sustained improvements in
the supervision the model produces.

## Appendix A Supplementary method details

### A.1 Training algorithm

Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ A.1 Training algorithm ‣ Appendix A Supplementary method details ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
summarizes offline initialization and the recurring online update. One
pre-update snapshot supplies the Actor, reflection generator, skill
generator, and skill-conditioned Teacher. The environmental estimator is
detailed in
Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Environmental advantage estimation ‣ Appendix A Supplementary method details ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents").

1: Initial policy $`\pi_{\theta_{0}}`$; offline R/S annotations
$`\mathcal{D}_{RS}`$; task sampler and environments; frozen reference
encoder; group size $`K=8`$; estimator and optimization settings

2: Trained Actor $`\pi_{\theta}`$ for inference with ordinary
interaction histories

3: Initialize shared parameters $`\theta`$ by R/S SFT on
$`\mathcal{D}_{RS}`$.

4: for each online iteration $`k`$ do

5:   Freeze snapshot
$`\theta_{k}\leftarrow\operatorname{stopgrad}(\theta)`$; sample task
batch $`\mathcal{X}_{k}`$; set $`\mathcal{B}_{k}\leftarrow\varnothing`$.

6:   Construct experience, Teacher guidance, and credit without
gradients.

7:   for each task $`x_{g}\in\mathcal{X}_{k}`$ do

8:    Collect $`K`$ trajectories $`\{\tau_{gj}\}_{j=1}^{K}`$ using
$`\pi_{\theta_{k}}`$.

9:    Record histories, responses, commands, rewards, outcomes, and old
token log probabilities.

10:    Compute the outcome-based GRPO advantages within task group
$`g`$.

11:    Sample reflections
$`u_{gj}\sim R_{\theta_{k}}(\cdot\mid x_{g},\tau_{gj},r_{gj})`$ for all
$`j`$.

12:    Sample one skill
$`z_{g}\sim S_{\theta_{k}}(\cdot\mid x_{g},\{u_{gj},r_{gj}\}_{j=1}^{K})`$.

13:    Record R/S prompts and pre-update log probabilities of their
sampled responses.

14:    Cluster observations using reference embeddings and identical
admissible-action sets.

15:    Build the transition graph; obtain $`\widehat{A}_{gjt}`$ by
Bellman evaluation, GAE, and normalization.

16:    Compute $`\delta_{gjt\ell}`$ on the same response and Actor
prefix, with/without $`z_{g}`$
(Equation [6](#S3.E6 "In 3.1 Preliminaries and shared-policy setup ‣ 3 Method ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")).

17:    Parse command positions $`\mathcal{C}_{gjt}`$; set
$`d_{gjt}\leftarrow\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{C}_{gjt}}\delta_{gjt\ell}`$.

18:    Set $`L_{gjt}\leftarrow|\mathcal{C}_{gjt}|`$ and
$`\bar{d}_{gjt}\leftarrow d_{gjt}/L_{gjt}`$; use zero for empty spans.

19:    Set $`q_{g}\leftarrow 0`$ for an all-success WebShop group and
$`q_{g}\leftarrow 1`$ otherwise.

20:
   $`m_{gjt}\leftarrow 1+\alpha_{m}\,\operatorname{sign}(\bar{d}_{gjt})\tanh\!\left(\widehat{A}_{gjt}/\kappa_{m}\right)`$.

21:
   $`w_{gjt\ell}\leftarrow q_{g}\,\mathbb{1}[\ell\in\mathcal{C}_{gjt}]\,m_{gjt}\delta_{gjt\ell}`$.

22:    Compute transition weights $`\omega_{i}`$ and state means
$`\overline{A}_{g}(s_{i})`$
(Equation [16](#S3.E16 "In 3.4 Credit for reflection and skill generation ‣ 3 Method ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")).

23:
   $`c_{g}\leftarrow\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{g}}\omega_{i}(\widehat{A}_{i}-\overline{A}_{g}(s_{i}))d_{i},-3,3\right)`$.

24:    Assign $`c_{g}`$ to all $`K`$ reflections and the skill; add the
group’s records to $`\mathcal{B}_{k}`$.

25:   end for

26:   Update the shared Actor and Analyzer.

27:   Form $`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}`$ on all valid Actor tokens and
$`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPSD}}`$ on commands using $`w`$.

28:   Form $`\mathcal{L}_{RS}`$ from credits $`c_{g}`$, with equal total
weight for R and S
(Equation [20](#S3.E20 "In 3.4 Credit for reflection and skill generation ‣ 3 Method ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")).

29:
  $`\mathcal{L}\leftarrow\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}+\beta_{T}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPSD}}+\beta_{RS}\mathcal{L}_{RS}`$
(Equation [21](#S3.E21 "In 3.5 Joint optimization and iterative updates ‣ 3 Method ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")).

30:   Optimize $`\mathcal{L}`$ over scheduled minibatches with
accumulated Actor and Analyzer gradients.

31: end for

32: return $`\pi_{\theta}`$ using ordinary histories at inference.

Algorithm 1 ECOS training

All old log probabilities, advantages, Teacher gaps, modulation weights,
and R/S credits remain fixed during optimization. The next iteration
regenerates experience and analysis using the updated parameters.

### A.2 Environmental advantage estimation

The estimator uses the representation-based grouping and empirical
Bellman evaluation described in
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Environmental command credit ‣ 3 Method ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents") \[[23](#bib.bib23);
[33](#bib.bib33)\]. Visits are processed in trajectory and turn order
after duplicate padding rows are removed. Only visits with identical
sorted admissible-action sets can share a cluster. Normalized
frozen-reference embeddings join the nearest normalized-centroid cluster
at cosine distance at most $`0.1`$; otherwise they form a new cluster.

Recorded commands define graph edges and retain the successor
observation and environmental reward. Rewards include the configured
invalid-action penalty of $`0.1`$. Initial values are mean observed
returns-to-go within each cluster.
Equation [8](#S3.E8 "In 3.2 Environmental command credit ‣ 3 Method ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
uses $`\gamma=0.95`$ and runs for at most twenty backups, stopping when
the largest value change is below $`10^{-6}`$. Terminal and horizon
successors have value zero.

The TD residuals enter the GAE recursion in
Equation [10](#S3.E10 "In 3.2 Environmental command credit ‣ 3 Method ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents"),
with $`\lambda_{\mathrm{GAE}}=0.8`$. After conversion to float32, group
normalization subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation
plus $`10^{-6}`$. Groups with standard deviation at most $`10^{-8}`$
receive zero auxiliary advantage. Clusters require at least two distinct
observed commands to contribute command credit. This estimator supplies
the auxiliary calibration and Analyzer terms; trajectory-level GRPO
retains its own outcome advantage.

### A.3 Modulation and state-centered credit

For $`0\leq\alpha_{m}\leq 1`$ and $`\kappa_{m}>0`$,
Equation [13](#S3.E13 "In 3.3 Environment-calibrated self-distillation ‣ 3 Method ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
satisfies

|     |                                          |     |       |
|-----|------------------------------------------|-----|-------|
|     |
       ``` math
       1-\alpha_{m}\leq m_{i}\leq 1+\alpha_{m}.
       ```                                       |     | (A.1) |

For $`\alpha_{m}>0`$, the multiplier exceeds one when
$`\bar{d}_{i}\widehat{A}_{i}>0`$ and is below one when
$`\bar{d}_{i}\widehat{A}_{i}<0`$. A zero environmental advantage gives
$`m_{i}=1`$. Command-level agreement therefore amplifies token-level
guidance, while command-level conflict attenuates it. The shared
nonnegative multiplier does not reverse individual token-gap directions.

Let $`W_{gs}=\sum_{i:s_{i}=s}\omega_{i}`$ and let $`\bar{d}_{g}(s)`$ be
the corresponding weighted mean of the raw summed command gaps. Since
the centered advantages sum to zero within a cluster,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle C_{g}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{s}\sum_{i:s_{i}=s}\omega_{i}(\widehat{A}_{i}-\overline{A}_{g}(s))(d_{i}-\bar{d}_{g}(s))`$ |  | (A.2) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{s}W_{gs}\,\operatorname{Cov}_{\omega}(\widehat{A},d\mid g,s).`$ |  | (A.3) |

The credit therefore rewards relative support for higher-advantage
commands within comparable states. Adding the same constant to all
command gaps in a cluster leaves $`C_{g}`$ unchanged. A cluster with no
advantage variation contributes zero. Each trajectory has equal total
weight, and its eligible commands divide that weight equally. Clipping
$`C_{g}`$ to $`[-3,3]`$ gives the reward used by both analysis stages.

## Appendix B Implementation and training

### B.1 Stage 1: supervised initialization of reflection and skill generation

Stage 1 trains the policy to produce reflections and reusable skills
before entering the online loop. It consists of offline trajectory
collection, annotation, and supervised fine-tuning.

#### Offline trajectory collection.

Each task-specific dataset contains 200 training tasks with eight
sampled trajectories per task, giving 1,600 trajectories. We retain the
task instruction, executed commands, observations, and recorded outcome
of each attempt. ALFWorld uses the corresponding Qwen2.5
instruction-tuned backbone for both collection and SFT initialization.
For WebShop, we collect trajectories from RL40 policies to obtain
sufficient successful and failed examples for SFT. The 3B run starts SFT
from Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, whereas the 7B run uses its GRPO40 policy for
both fresh trajectory collection and SFT initialization.

#### Reflection and skill annotation.

An external annotator reads each task and its recorded interaction, then
writes a reflection grounded in the actions, observations, and outcome.
Successful and failed attempts provide examples of useful decisions and
mistakes to correct, respectively. The eight reflections are then
supplied together with the task to produce one consolidated skill. This
yields 1,600 reflection targets and 200 skill targets per dataset. All
offline annotations use GPT-6.1 sol with maximum reasoning effort.
Appendix [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Reflection and skill prompts ‣ Appendix B Implementation and training ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
shows the R/S prompt structure and recorded examples.

#### Supervised examples and optimization.

Each task group contributes nine input–target pairs. A reflection input
contains the task and one recorded trajectory with its outcome; the
target is that trajectory’s annotated reflection. The skill input
contains the task and all eight annotated reflections; its target is the
consolidated skill. We apply the backbone’s chat template and train with
teacher forcing over the saved target tokens. Task instructions and
interaction histories supply conditioning context, while the loss covers
the reflection or skill target.

For a target sequence $`y`$ with input $`x`$, let
$`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NLL}}(y\mid x)`$ denote its mean autoregressive
negative log-likelihood. For task group $`g`$, the offline reflection
and skill targets are $`u_{gj}`$ and $`z_{g}`$. The task-group objective
is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(g)=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{1}{8}\sum_{j=1}^{8}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NLL}}(u_{gj}\mid x^{R}_{gj})+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NLL}}(z_{g}\mid x^{S}_{g})\right].
``` |  | (B.1) |

Thus the eight reflections jointly receive half of the group weight and
skill synthesis receives the other half. Gradients from all nine
examples accumulate before one optimizer update. We fine-tune all
parameters for three epochs, shuffling task groups each epoch, for a
total of 600 updates. The resulting SFT600 weights initialize the shared
Actor and Analyzer in Stage 2.
Table [B.1](#A2.T1 "Table B.1 ‣ Supervised examples and optimization. ‣ B.1 Stage 1: supervised initialization of reflection and skill generation ‣ Appendix B Implementation and training ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
summarizes the optimization settings.

| Hyperparameter |  Value |
|----|----|
| Training tasks / trajectories per task |  200 / 8 |
| Supervised targets |  1,600 reflections and 200 skills |
| Batch per optimizer update |  1 task group: 8 reflections and 1 skill |
| Reflection / skill loss weights |  $`0.5`$ / $`0.5`$ |
| Epochs / optimizer updates |  3 / 600 |
| Trainable parameters |  Full model |
| Optimizer |  AdamW |
| Learning rate |  $`5\times 10^{-6}`$ |
| Adam $`(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})`$ / $`\epsilon`$ |  $`(0.9,0.999)`$ / $`10^{-8}`$ |
| Weight decay / gradient norm limit |  $`0`$ / $`1.0`$ |
| Learning-rate schedule / warmup |  Constant / 0 steps |
| Parameter and optimizer precision |  FP32 |
| Forward-pass precision |  BF16 autocast |
| Training seed |  0 |

Table B.1: Stage 1 SFT settings, shared across the four task/model
configurations.

All experiments were conducted on a server equipped with eight NVIDIA

and evaluation.

### B.4 Token masks and joint optimization

Command-content masks select the parsed command span, excluding
reasoning, delimiter tags, observations, and padding. The primary policy
loss and regularization use all valid generated response tokens. Teacher
scoring retains the Actor’s sampled reasoning prefix. Only command
tokens receive the direct OPSD term. The mean command gap
$`\bar{d}_{gjt}`$ determines a shared modulation multiplier, which
scales each command token’s own gap $`\delta_{gjt\ell}`$, with the same
token-mean loss reduction.

Analyzer credit uses raw summed command gaps $`d_{gjt}`$ before
modulation.
Equation [20](#S3.E20 "In 3.4 Credit for reflection and skill generation ‣ 3 Method ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
gives equal total weight to reflection and skill generation and averages
each generated sequence over its own valid tokens. Zero-credit groups
remain in the fixed group denominator. Actor and Analyzer gradients
share the scheduled AdamW updates, with no additional R/S optimizer
steps.

## Appendix C Baselines, benchmarks, and evaluation setting

### C.1 Baseline details

Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Overall agent performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
compares Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct models. We
summarize the baseline variants reported by
AlignOPSD \[[6](#bib.bib6)\]. An asterisk denotes retrieved-skill access
at inference; unmarked methods receive only the task prompt and
interaction history.

- •
  Vanilla. The instruction-tuned backbone acts directly in the
  environment without additional task-specific training.
- •
  Skill-Prompt\*. A retrieved task-relevant skill is added to Vanilla’s
  context at validation and test time.
- •
  GRPO \[[22](#bib.bib22)\]. Terminal rewards are normalized within each
  task group to obtain trajectory advantages, which supervise the
  sampled response tokens without a learned critic.
- •
  Skill-GRPO / Skill-GRPO\*. Both variants condition GRPO training on
  retrieved skills. Evaluation removes the skills for Skill-GRPO and
  retains them for Skill-GRPO\*.
- •
  OPSD \[[7](#bib.bib7)\]. A privileged-context Teacher re-scores tokens
  from student-generated trajectories, providing detached token-level
  supervision. The student learns to reproduce these preferences using
  its ordinary interaction context.
- •
  GRPO+OPSD. A joint objective combines terminal-reward GRPO advantages
  with token-level supervision from the privileged-context Teacher.
- •
  Skill-SD \[[9](#bib.bib9)\]. Skills condition the Teacher alone, and
  importance-weighted distillation transfers its guidance to the acting
  policy.
- •
  RLSD. Teacher–Student information produces a bounded scaling
  coefficient for GRPO updates. The outcome advantage determines the
  direction of each scaled update.
- •
  SDAR \[[18](#bib.bib18)\]. A gate regulates an auxiliary
  self-distillation loss alongside GRPO, while the original
  environmental advantage estimate is retained.
- •
  AlignOPSD \[[6](#bib.bib6)\]. Cross-rollout decision correspondence
  rectifies Teacher supervision, while adaptive decision spans and
  hierarchical credit assignment allocate the resulting guidance.
- •
  Ours. Task-specific R/S SFT initializes a shared Actor and Analyzer.
  Environmental command advantages calibrate signed Teacher preferences
  on executable command tokens. State-centered credit trains reflections
  and skills, linking Teacher construction to subsequent policy updates.
  Inference uses the trained Actor with the ordinary task prompt and
  interaction history.

The published baseline values are taken from AlignOPSD
Table 1 \[[6](#bib.bib6)\].
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Implementation and training ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
specifies our initialization and training settings; the following
subsections describe our task panels, inference settings, and reporting
conventions.

### C.2 Task panels and metrics

ALFWorld evaluation covers all 140 seen and 134 unseen tasks.
Table [C.1](#A3.T1 "Table C.1 ‣ C.2 Task panels and metrics ‣ Appendix C Baselines, benchmarks, and evaluation setting ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
gives the six category sizes. If $`k_{c}`$ of $`n_{c}`$ tasks succeed in
category $`c`$, macro success is
$`\frac{100}{6}\sum_{c=1}^{6}k_{c}/n_{c}`$. Each category therefore
contributes equally. Success is determined by the first terminal
environment outcome.

|  Split   | Pick | Look | Clean | Heat | Cool | Pick2 | Total |
|----------|------|------|-------|------|------|-------|-------|
|  Seen    | 35   | 13   | 27    | 16   | 25   | 24    | 140   |
|  Unseen  | 24   | 18   | 31    | 23   | 21   | 17    | 134   |

Table C.1: ALFWorld evaluation tasks by category.

WebShop uses 128 goals sampled without replacement. Our repeated
evaluations draw a 128-goal panel for each evaluation seed; methods
using the same seed share the panel. The catalogue seed remains 0, with
the training-compatible search index of 1,000 products. Success is the
percentage of tasks completed fully. Score is the mean normalized
terminal environment reward multiplied by 100, capturing partial
satisfaction of the requested product attributes.

### C.3 Inference settings

Evaluation uses temperature $`0.4`$, top-$`p=1`$, top-$`k=-1`$, and one
trajectory per task. The Actor receives the ordinary task prompt and
interaction history, without appended skills or online R/S generation.
ALFWorld allows at most 30 actions with history length five; WebShop
allows at most 15 actions with history length two. Prompt and response
limits follow
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Implementation and training ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents").
Infrastructure errors are recorded separately from completed task
failures.

### C.4 Reporting conventions

All task-performance results for our method and its ablations use the
final checkpoint after 150 online updates. The 134-task unseen split is
used only for final evaluation.

All training runs use a fixed random seed. After training, each
checkpoint is evaluated under three evaluation seeds, and we report the
mean and standard deviation in
Tables [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Overall agent performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
and [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ The gains extend to unseen task instances. ‣ 4.2 Overall agent performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents").

The local GRPO baselines in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ The gains extend to unseen task instances. ‣ 4.2 Overall agent performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
use the same initialization, task sampling, rollout budget, Actor
optimization settings, and evaluation protocol as the full method in
Table [B.2](#A2.T2 "Table B.2 ‣ B.2 Stage 2: online optimization ‣ Appendix B Implementation and training ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents").
Their online updates optimize $`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}`$ alone,
including the same reference-policy KL penalty and entropy bonus, for
150 updates. They are evaluated on the same unseen task panel with the
same inference settings as our models.

The GRPO row in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.4 Ablation study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
repeats the published baseline values quoted in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Overall agent performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents").
Published baseline numbers come from Table 1 of
AlignOPSD \[[6](#bib.bib6)\] and retain their source aggregation.

### C.5 Ablation configurations and evaluation

Table [C.2](#A3.T2 "Table C.2 ‣ Full-response supervision in variant (b). ‣ C.5 Ablation configurations and evaluation ‣ Appendix C Baselines, benchmarks, and evaluation setting ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
specifies the full method and the three 3B ablation variants. All
variants generate eight reflections and one skill per task group during
online training. Variant (a) omits R/S SFT and starts from
Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. Variant (b) extends direct Teacher supervision to
the complete response, including reasoning. Variant (c) retains
command-only supervision and online R/S generation in both environments;
it sets the modulation multiplier to one and removes the direct R/S
objective. The remaining settings follow
Table [B.2](#A2.T2 "Table B.2 ‣ B.2 Stage 2: online optimization ‣ Appendix B Implementation and training ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents").

#### Full-response supervision in variant (b).

At each interaction turn, we compute the modulation multiplier
$`m_{gjt}`$ from the executable command’s mean gap $`\bar{d}_{gjt}`$ and
environmental advantage $`\widehat{A}_{gjt}`$ using
Equation [13](#S3.E13 "In 3.3 Environment-calibrated self-distillation ‣ 3 Method ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents").
This multiplier is broadcast to all valid generated tokens in the same
Actor response, including reasoning and command content. Each token
retains its own Teacher–Actor gap, giving

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
w^{(b)}_{gjt\ell}=q_{g}\,m_{gjt}\,\delta_{gjt\ell},\qquad(g,j,t,\ell)\in\mathcal{B}_{A}.
``` |  | (C.1) |

The loss uses the clipped token objective in
Equation [14](#S3.E14 "In 3.3 Environment-calibrated self-distillation ‣ 3 Method ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents").
Both supervision scopes use the Actor token-mean denominator
$`|\mathcal{B}_{A}|`$ in
Equation [15](#S3.E15 "In 3.3 Environment-calibrated self-distillation ‣ 3 Method ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents"),
Teacher coefficient $`\beta_{T}=0.01`$, and PPO clipping ratio $`0.2`$.
The full-response branch applies these token-level Teacher terms
throughout the sampled response under the command-derived multiplier.

| Variant | SFT | Scope    | Mod. |  R/S loss  |  Online R/S  |
|---------|-----|----------|------|------------|--------------|
| Full    | Yes | Command  | Yes  | Yes        | Yes          |
| \(a\)   | No  | Command  | Yes  | Yes        | Yes          |
| \(b\)   | Yes | Response | Yes  | Yes        | Yes          |
| \(c\)   | Yes | Command  | No   | No         | Yes          |

Table C.2: Training components used in the ablation study. Scope denotes
the tokens covered by direct Teacher supervision. Online R/S denotes
reflection and skill generation during training.

Each branch trains for 150 online updates and is evaluated at its final
checkpoint. ALFWorld evaluation uses all 140 seen tasks, at most 30
actions, and history length five. WebShop evaluation uses the fixed
128-task panel, at most 15 actions, and history length two. Both
environments use temperature $`0.4`$ and one trajectory per task. We
report six-category macro success for ALFWorld and Score and Success for
WebShop. The GRPO row contains the published baseline values described
above.

## Appendix D Mechanistic analysis and training dynamics

### D.1 Paired measurement of Teacher weight

The analysis in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Mechanistic analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")(a,b)
uses recorded command spans, likelihood gaps, modulation weights, and
primary policy advantages from the two 3B runs specified in
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Stage 2: online optimization ‣ Appendix B Implementation and training ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents").
We recorded nine snapshots per environment. Duplicate padding rows are
removed, and each executed command contributes one observation. We
retain commands with an active Teacher span and a primary advantage
satisfying $`|\widehat{A}_{i}^{\mathrm{RL}}|>10^{-8}`$. The same
commands are used before and after modulation.

The raw command coefficient is the summed Teacher–Actor gap $`d_{i}`$.
The final command coefficient is the mean saved coefficient over the
command’s content tokens. These command-level values enter the
reward-alignment statistic in
Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Mechanistic analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents").
Each condition is normalized by its own total absolute coefficient mass.
This comparison includes both command-length normalization and
environmental modulation. The shaded region in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Mechanistic analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")(a,b)
shows the paired percentage-point difference.

The reference advantage $`\widehat{A}_{i}^{\mathrm{RL}}`$ comes from the
primary policy objective: the recorded outcome includes the configured
invalid-command penalty and is standardized within the task group. The
auxiliary graph advantage $`\widehat{A}_{i}`$ determines modulation. The
primary advantage provides the outcome-derived reference for the
measurement, and the auxiliary advantage controls the Teacher
multiplier.

### D.2 Return concordance of skill-induced preferences

For each skill, we pair distinct commands from different trajectories
when their stored Actor prompts and admissible-action sets match
exactly. Teacher scoring retains the reasoning prefix sampled in each
response. Let $`\Delta d_{ij}=d_{i}-d_{j}`$ be the difference in raw
command gaps and $`\Delta R_{ij}=R_{i}-R_{j}`$ the difference in
recorded returns-to-go. Pairs with $`|\Delta R_{ij}|\leq 10^{-8}`$ are
omitted. With $`\varepsilon=10^{-8}`$, the pair score is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
h_{ij}=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2},&|\Delta d_{ij}|\leq\varepsilon,\\
1,&|\Delta d_{ij}|>\varepsilon\ \text{and}\ \Delta d_{ij}\Delta R_{ij}>0,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (D.1) |

Concordance is $`100`$ times the mean pair score within a skill. Skills
with at least one eligible pair enter the analysis. We then give each
skill equal weight, so skills with more observed command pairs do not
dominate the comparison.

The pooled analysis uses the saved snapshots after the initial update.
Within each task, the median bounded R/S credit $`c_{g}`$ separates the
higher- and lower-credit groups; median ties belong to the lower-credit
group.
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Mechanistic analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")(c,d)
displays individual skills, group means, and interquartile ranges. The
complete measurements underlying the figure accompany the supplementary
data.

Figures [D.1](#A4.F1 "Figure D.1 ‣ D.3 Training dynamics ‣ Appendix D Mechanistic analysis and training dynamics ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
and [D.2](#A4.F2 "Figure D.2 ‣ D.3 Training dynamics ‣ Appendix D Mechanistic analysis and training dynamics ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents")
show the 3B and 7B command-only runs over 150 updates. Success and
interaction length summarize 128 trajectories per update;
positive-credit fractions count all sixteen skills, including
zero-credit groups. Modulation coverage retains the logged
training-batch rows and active-Teacher mask.

Figure D.1: Training dynamics of the 3B agents. Columns show ALFWorld
and WebShop; rows show training success, modulated-action coverage, the
fraction of skills receiving positive R/S credit, and mean interaction
length. Light curves show individual updates; dark curves show trailing
ten-update means, using available updates at the start. Success rises
and episodes shorten while environmental feedback continues to select
and modulate supervision.

Figure D.2: Training dynamics of the 7B agents. Columns and rows follow
Figure [D.1](#A4.F1 "Figure D.1 ‣ D.3 Training dynamics ‣ Appendix D Mechanistic analysis and training dynamics ‣ ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents"),
with the same axis ranges and moving-average convention. Both tasks show
increasing success and shorter interactions. Modulation coverage remains
active on ALFWorld and declines on WebShop.
````
